extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science; journalists and public men
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating newspapers as organs of opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the roles, functions, and qualities of newspapers and other organs in expressing and shaping public opinion in the United States—covering accuracy, advocacy, reach, independence, and electoral influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of newspaper influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers are influential in three ways — as narrators, as advocates, and as weathercocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrators: report events; Advocates: advance arguments; Weathercocks: indicate by attitude what those who conduct them take to be the prevailing opinion of their readers. Use all three roles to judge a paper's overall influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual accuracy and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: The American press is apt to describe occurrences which may possibly have happened, however slight the evidence for them; this habit affects its worth as an historic record and its influence with sober-minded people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate speed-versus-veracity trade-offs: high-pressure, competitive reporting often yields erroneous statements. Anti-pattern: once an untrue story is set flying, its effect is hard to efface even with complete contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism versus sober reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The appetite for news and for highly spiced or 'sensation' news is enormous, and journalists working under keen competition and in unceasing haste take their chance of the correctness of the information they receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure a paper's tendency toward sensationalism (negative) against its capacity to attract attention and expose wrongdoers (positive). Excessive sensationalism undermines historical worth and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watchdog / investigative function
rubrics_metrics.description: The press is a watch-dog whose noisy bark must be tolerated; it exposes evil-doers and prevents many abuses by the fear of publicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess effectiveness at exposing corruption and prompting reform. Recognize that this function may cause pain to innocents but yields public benefits by uncovering abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisanship and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Partizanship distorts it no more than in Europe; American papers are less markedly party organs than British ones and leading articles carry less independent weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge degree of party alignment. Independent or semi-independent journals may be more useful indicators of real popular strength; party journals can signal party strategy rather than mass opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasiveness of editorials
rubrics_metrics.description: A leading article carries less weight of itself, being discounted by the shrewd reader, and is effective only when it takes hold of some fact (real or supposed) and hammers it into the public mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate editorials by their evidentiary grounding and ability to connect argument to salient facts; mere abuse or declamation is less effective long-term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness as index and mirror of public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The press serves chiefly as an index and mirror of public opinion — indicating which views have popular strength behind them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether coverage reflects a broad cross-section of views or the views of particular groups; treat professed party organs with caution when inferring mass sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to shape opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: An organ of public opinion is not merely the expression of views already in existence, but a factor in further developing and moulding the judgment of the people — 'opinion makes opinion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure a paper's agenda-setting and bandwagon effects: how its voices create momentum for particular views or candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation, reach, and market concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: The vast area of the republic and absence of a capital prevent any one paper from winning predominance; twenty American papers would not cover one-third of the reading public, unlike in England where a few journals cover nine-tenths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate geographic reach and market concentration: broad national influence requires wide circulation or dominant regional position; many competing papers dilute single-paper dominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition and multiplicity of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: In cities most people look at more than one newspaper; strong papers are exposed to severer competition than in Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how competition affects quality (more cross-checking) and reduces the ability of any single paper to monopolize opinion; competition can both improve factualness and increase haste-driven errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prominent individuals' statements (private deliverances, interviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans cite private deliverances of prominent men (letters, announced votes, interviews) as an organ for catching, measuring, and indicating opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the reliability and intentionality of such signals: they can be engineered to influence public perception, and interviews/letters offer opportunities for later disavowal or clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of journals and differential influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Three classes of semi-independent journals: (1) papers generally supporting one party but liable to fly off, (2) papers mainly devoted to news, (3) papers not primarily political (e.g., religious weeklies) which may have great moral influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider genre when assessing influence: religious weeklies and magazines may exert strong moral authority (especially when read on Sunday), while news-focused papers influence via breadth of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role during electoral contests
rubrics_metrics.description: During presidential contests much importance is attributed to the attitude of the leading papers of great cities; the revolt of prominent papers indicates discontent and danger for parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate newspapers' electoral cues: endorsements, schisms, and city-paper revolts as indicators of party health and shifts in mass sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Susceptibility to local or factional capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a schism exists in a State party, bosses will sometimes try to capture and manipulate smaller country papers to convey the impression that their faction is gaining ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess vulnerability of smaller/local papers to manipulation by political actors; beware of manufactured impressions of momentum originating from captured press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of the press as sole gauge of sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: The journals seem to convey what their writers wish to be believed, and not necessarily what the people are really thinking; prudent men keep a circle of discerning friends to test impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the press in conjunction with direct conversation, meetings, and local observation to avoid being misled by editorial agendas or local biases; treat press-derived impressions as suggestive rather than definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and nature of public meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Except during electoral campaigns public meetings play a smaller part in the U.S. than in Western Europe; meetings are usually held for practical objects (candidate selection, organization) rather than as mere demonstrations or instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating public sentiment from meetings, recognize their functional/practical character in the U.S.; they may show organizational strength more than argumentative persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of public argument and speaking
rubrics_metrics.description: There are fewer reports of speeches of an argumentative nature in America, but more of the schemes and doings of conventions and political cliques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the depth of public debate: quantity of speeches does not equal quality of argument; focus on venues and occasions where reasoned argument is more likely (e.g., lectures, certain magazines).
